mcqs.question: What is the key architectural reason two-tower models keep the user and item networks separate instead of combining features early, as neural collaborative filtering does?
options: Separate towers train faster because they have fewer total parameters than a combined network
It lets item embeddings be precomputed offline for the entire catalog, turning serving-time scoring into a fast nearest-neighbor lookup rather than a forward pass per candidate
It's required because user and item features must always live in different vector spaces
Combining features early would make the model unable to learn non-linear interactions
mcqs.explanation: Keeping the towers independent is what makes item embeddings precomputable ahead of time, which is the entire scaling trick — serving becomes ANN search, not per-candidate inference. Parameter count isn't the driver, the two towers actually share the same embedding space by design, and non-linearity is achieved within each tower regardless.

mcqs.question: Why don't two-tower or NCF-style deep recommenders automatically solve the cold-start problem just by being more powerful models?
options: Because deep networks are too slow to serve for cold-start users
Because cold start only affects matrix factorization, not neural architectures

Because a collaborative ID embedding still has no learned signal for a user or item with zero interaction history, regardless of the model's depth — content features have to be added deliberately to fill that gap
Because two-tower models cannot output embeddings for items added after training
mcqs.explanation: The limitation is about signal, not model capacity — an ID embedding for a brand-new item is simply untrained, no matter how expressive the surrounding network is. The fix is architectural (add content features), not a matter of scale. Cold start affects all purely collaborative methods, and two-tower models can score new items fine once given content features, even without retraining the ID embedding.

mcqs.question: Why do two-tower models commonly use 'in-batch negatives' rather than sampling separate negative examples for every training pair?
options: Because it provides negatives essentially for free by reusing the other items already loaded in the same training batch, avoiding the cost of separately fetching negatives for every example at catalog scale
Because in-batch negatives are more accurate labels than explicitly sampled negatives
Because sampling separate negatives is mathematically impossible for two-tower architectures
Because in-batch negatives eliminate the need for a loss function
mcqs.explanation: The appeal is purely computational efficiency: items already in the batch double as free negatives, sidestepping the cost of fetching separate negative samples at catalog scale. In-batch negatives aren't inherently 'more accurate' labels (they're a practical proxy, hence the popularity correction needed), separate sampling is entirely possible (just costlier), and a loss function is still required either way.

mcqs.question: What is the main advantage of a multi-task ranking model with shared layers and separate output heads, over training entirely separate models for each objective?
options: It requires no labeled data at all for any of the objectives
It always makes each individual objective's prediction more accurate than a dedicated single-task model would
Shared layers learn a general representation once, while separate heads specialize per objective, letting the final score be a tunable combination rather than relying on any single proxy label alone
It eliminates the need to choose a combination weighting between objectives at serving time
mcqs.explanation: The value is architectural efficiency and directly addressing the single-proxy-label problem: one shared representation feeds multiple specialized heads, and the final score deliberately combines several signals rather than trusting one. Labeled data is still needed per objective, a multi-task model isn't guaranteed to beat a dedicated single-task model on every individual objective, and a combination weighting still has to be chosen and tuned.

mcqs.question: Why might switching from matrix factorization to a deeper neural recommender make popularity bias worse rather than better, if nothing else changes?
options: Deep models automatically detect and correct for popularity bias as part of training
Popularity bias only exists in matrix factorization, not in neural architectures
Deep models cannot process popular items at all
The extra capacity lets the model fit the already-skewed logged interaction data more precisely, reinforcing the over-representation of popular items rather than correcting for it
mcqs.explanation: More capacity means a better fit to whatever data it's given, and if that data already over-represents popular items, a deeper model can fit — and thus reinforce — that skew more precisely, not correct it. Nothing about deep architectures inherently debiases training data, popular items are of course processed (just over-weighted), and this bias applies broadly across collaborative methods, not just matrix factorization.
